subject: Art & Design
title: Designing for Color Blindness
description: A micro-lesson that makes Designing for Color Blindness usable.

hook.text: 8% of men are red-green color blind. If your error states are red-only, millions of users can't see them.

buildup.text: Color blindness means certain colors appear identical. Red/green confusion is most common.

discovery.text: Never use color as the only indicator. Add icons, patterns, labels, or borders alongside color signals.

twist.text: Tools like Sim Daltonism and Stark simulate color blindness. Test your designs — what you see isn't universal.

climax.text: Accessible color design isn't a niche concern. With 300 million color-blind people, it's mainstream.

punchline.text: Good design works for everyone's eyes, not just yours.

quiz.question: Why should color never be the only indicator of meaning?
options: 8% of men are color blind and may not distinguish the colors
Colors look different on every screen

details.summary: Approximately 8% of men and 0.5% of women have some form of color vision deficiency. Designs that rely solely on color to convey meaning — red vs. green status indicators — exclude millions. Accessible design adds shape, pattern, or text labels alongside color to ensure information reaches everyone.
details.whyItMatters: Designing only for full-color vision excludes roughly 300 million people worldwide. Color-blind-friendly design isn't specialized accessibility work — it's basic design competence that improves usability for everyone.
takeaways: About 8% of men have some color vision deficiency
Designs must not rely on color alone to convey meaning
Adding shapes, patterns, or labels ensures universal access

faq.question: What type of color blindness is most common?
faq.answer: Red-green color blindness (deuteranopia/protanopia) accounts for about 99% of cases. People with this condition struggle to distinguish red from green, making traffic-light-style status indicators problematic. Using blue/orange instead of red/green is one simple solution.

faq.question: How can designers test for color blindness issues?
faq.answer: Tools like Sim Daltonism, Coblis, and built-in browser developer tools simulate different color vision deficiencies. Figma and Adobe also offer color-blind simulation modes. The simplest test: convert the design to grayscale. If information is lost, the design relies too heavily on color.
